44206: Jesus heals the blind as a sign of spiritual sight; the Lamb has seven eyes, the seven spirits sent into all the earth (Rev 5:6).
44208: In the Bible the heart is not mainly about feelings. It is the centre of the whole person: thinking, choosing, desiring and loving. What is in the heart shapes everything a person does, which is why God looks at the heart and promises to give a new one.
44209: The control centre of the person
44210: Evil and good flow out of the heart; God looks on the heart, not outward appearance.
44211: Corrupted and in need of renewal
44212: God promises to write his law on hearts and replace a heart of stone.
44214: Love God with all your heart.
44215: True belonging to God is inward, a heart opened to him.
44217: Pharaoh hardens his heart and God hardens it; how these relate is debated (see /debates/soteriology).
44219: God's love and Spirit are poured into the heart; Christ dwells there by faith.
44220: Lev and levav occur hundreds of times. For deep emotions Hebrew often uses other organs, such as the kidneys (translated 'mind' or 'reins', Ps 7:9; Jer 17:10) and the bowels (Isa 63:15).
44221: Jesus locates purity and sin in the heart (Matt 5:8; Matt 15:19). Paul says belief happens with the heart (Rom 10:9-10).
44222: Modern 'follow your heart' advice means trusting one's feelings; the Bible both honours the heart and warns that it can deceive (Jer 17:9). Do not read the modern meaning back into biblical texts.
44225: The head is the top and front of the body. In the Bible it can mean leader or chief, the beginning or source, and the place where honour, blessing or shame are shown.
44227: Israel will be 'the head and not the tail'; Jephthah is made head over Gilead.
44228: Christ as head of the church and of all things
44229: The body grows from and under its head.
44231: Whether kephale here means 'authority over' or 'source/origin' (or both) is a key point in /debates/gender-roles, with careful scholars on each side.
44232: Blessing and honour on the head
44233: Blessings and anointing oil rest on the head.
44235: Dust on the head and covered heads show grief; 'his blood be on his own head' means he bears responsibility.
44236: The 'head of the corner' (Ps 118:22), heads of families and tribes, and the shaved or covered head in mourning.
44237: Christ's headship over the church, the head-covering discussion of 1 Corinthians 11, and Jesus having 'nowhere to lay his head' (Matt 8:20).
44238: Whether the head coverings of 1 Corinthians 11:4-16 are a timeless rule or a cultural application of a principle is debated.
44241: Feet carry people along their way, get dirty, and are the lowest part of the body. In the Bible they picture how one lives, humble service, submission, and victory over enemies placed 'under the feet'.
44243: Enemies are made a footstool; Satan will be crushed under believers' feet.
44245: Washing feet was slaves' work; Jesus does it for his disciples.
44246: The posture of a disciple or worshipper
44247: Sitting at someone's feet means learning from them; falling at their feet means worship or surrender.
44249: The feet of those who bring good news are beautiful.
44252: Hospitality began with washing guests' feet; enemies were trodden underfoot; Ruth lay at Boaz's feet (Ruth 3:7-8).
44253: Mary sits at Jesus' feet; a sinful woman anoints them; Jesus washes the disciples' feet; the risen Christ's feet are like burnished bronze (Rev 1:15).
44254: Hebrew sometimes uses 'feet' as a polite euphemism for private parts (probably Isa 7:20). Whether Ruth 3 or Exodus 4:25 has this sense is debated; avoid building conclusions on it.
44256: Blood is life: when it is poured out, a creature dies. So in the Bible blood means life given up in death. It cries out when murder is done, and it makes atonement when offered in sacrifice. The New Testament centres on the blood of Jesus.
44258: Blood was not to be eaten because the life is in it.
44259: God gave blood on the altar to make atonement. How Christ's blood atones is explained differently by the various atonement views (see /debates/atonement).
44261: Passover blood marked the houses; Moses sprinkled 'the blood of the covenant'; Jesus speaks of his blood of the new covenant.
44263: Christ's blood buys people for God from every nation and washes robes white.
44265: Abel's blood cries out for justice; Jesus' blood 'speaks a better word'.
44266: Water turned to blood; the moon turned to blood.
44267: Sacrifices, the Passover, covenant-making, food laws and laws on murder all centre on blood.
44268: The Lord's Supper cup, Jesus' death, the Jerusalem council's ban on eating blood for Gentile believers (Acts 15:20), and Revelation's praise of the Lamb's blood.
44269: Matthew 27:25 ('his blood be on us and on our children') was misused for centuries to blame Jews collectively for Jesus' death; Christian churches, including the Catholic Church at Vatican II (*Nostra Aetate* 4), have rejected that reading. 'Pleading the blood' as a spoken formula is a later devotional practice, not a biblical one.
44272: Seeing someone's face means being in their presence and knowing them personally. In Hebrew the word for 'face' also means 'presence'. God's shining face means his favour; his hidden face means distance and trouble. The hope of the Bible is to see God face to face.
44273: 'My presence (literally, my face) will go with you.'
44275: 'Make your face shine on us, and we shall be saved.'
44277: The LORD spoke to Moses 'face to face', yet Moses could not see God's face and live. 'Face to face' is an idiom of direct, personal relationship.
44279: Moses' face shone; believers are transformed as they behold the Lord's glory in the face of Christ.
44282: The 'bread of the Presence' is literally 'bread of the face'. Jacob names a place Peniel ('face of God', Gen 32:30). Psalms of lament ask why God hides his face.
44283: Jesus 'set his face' to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51); his face shines at the transfiguration; angels always see the Father's face (Matt 18:10).
44285: A bared, outstretched arm is a picture of strength put to work. 'The arm of the LORD' means God personally stepping in with power to rescue his people, as he did in the exodus.
44287: 'With a mighty hand and an outstretched arm.'
44289: God bares his holy arm before all nations; when no one else could save, his own arm brought salvation.
44291: Isaiah asks 'to whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed?' just before describing the suffering servant; John applies this to Jesus. Many read the servant himself as the arm revealed; others read the arm as God's power shown through him.
44293: The same arm that rules gathers lambs; 'underneath are the everlasting arms'.
44294: Not trusting in an 'arm of flesh'
44295: Human strength is contrasted with God's.
44296: Mostly in the exodus traditions, the Psalms and Isaiah 40 to 66.
44297: Mary sings that God 'has shown strength with his arm' (Luke 1:51); Paul says God led Israel out of Egypt 'with an uplifted arm' (Acts 13:17).
44298: Like 'hand' and 'face', this is a figure of speech for God's action, not a claim that God has a physical body.
44301: Gold is the most precious and lasting metal, and it does not tarnish. In the Bible it marks God's glory and dwelling, royal wealth, faith refined by testing, and also the greed and idolatry that wealth can lead to.
44303: The ark, mercy seat, lampstand and inner temple were gold; the new Jerusalem is pure gold like glass.
44305: Nations bring gold to the king; the Magi bring gold to Jesus. Early tradition read gold as honouring him as king (Irenaeus, *Against Heresies* 3.9.2).
44308: The golden calf; Achan's stolen gold; idols of silver and gold.
44309: Wisdom and God's word worth more than gold
44310: The truly valuable things outweigh gold.
44311: Tabernacle and temple furnishings, Solomon's wealth, Nebuchadnezzar's head of gold (Dan 2:38) and his golden statue.
44312: The Magi's gift, warnings about wealth, refined faith, golden lampstands and bowls in Revelation, and the golden city.
44313: Typological systems that make gold always mean 'divinity' go beyond the text; context decides.
44316: Silver was the everyday money of the ancient world, weighed out in shekels. So in the Bible it often means price and payment, including the price of redemption, and it is used as a picture of refining and purity.
44318: Joseph is sold for twenty pieces of silver; Jesus is betrayed for thirty.
44320: Israelites paid silver as a ransom for their lives; Peter says believers were redeemed not with silver or gold but with Christ's blood.
44322: God's words are like silver refined seven times.
44325: Tabernacle bases cast from ransom silver
44326: The silver from the census ransom was cast into the sockets that held up the tabernacle. Seeing this as 'the house of God resting on redemption' is a later typological reading.
44327: Trade, temple furnishings, ransom payments, and the second-ranked kingdom in Nebuchadnezzar's statue (Dan 2:32).
44328: Judas' thirty pieces, Peter's 'silver and gold I do not have' (Acts 3:6), and the silversmiths of Ephesus (Acts 19:24).
44329: Saying 'silver always means redemption' is a later typological habit; most uses are simply about money.
44331: Bronze (an alloy of copper and tin) was strong and used for tools, weapons and the outer furnishings of the tabernacle. It is associated with strength, endurance, and the places where sin was dealt with: the altar and the bronze serpent.
44332: The place of sacrifice and cleansing
44333: The altar of burnt offering and the washing basin in the courtyard were bronze. Reading bronze as a code for 'judgement' is a later typological convention.
44334: The bronze serpent: healing by looking
44335: Bitten Israelites looked at the bronze serpent and lived; Jesus compares his being 'lifted up'.
44336: A good sign turned into an idol
44337: Hezekiah smashed the bronze serpent (Nehushtan) because people were burning incense to it.
44341: The risen Christ's feet are like burnished bronze refined in a furnace.
44342: Tabernacle courtyard, Solomon's great bronze pillars and sea (1 Kgs 7:13-47), Goliath's armour, and the drought curse of skies like bronze (Deut 28:23).
44343: Jesus' reference to the bronze serpent and Revelation's description of his feet.
44344: KJV 'brass' (copper and zinc) is a mistranslation by modern standards; the ancient metal was copper or bronze.
44346: Iron was the hard, new metal of the Iron Age and gave military advantage. In the Bible it pictures crushing strength, unbreakable rule, harsh oppression and stubbornness.
44348: The fourth kingdom is iron that breaks everything, yet mixed with clay. Most identify it with Rome (traditional) or with the Greek kingdoms (many modern scholars).
44350: The Messiah rules with a rod of iron.
44352: Egypt was an 'iron furnace'; a yoke of iron is crushing slavery.
44354: Canaanite iron chariots and the Philistine monopoly on smithing.
44356: A neck like an iron sinew; 'iron sharpens iron'.
44357: Og's iron bed (Deut 3:11), tools that were not to touch the altar stones (Deut 27:5), and Elisha's floating axe head (2 Kgs 6:5-7).
44358: Mostly Revelation's rod of iron and the iron gate that opens for Peter (Acts 12:10).
44361: Gems are rare, beautiful and lasting. In the Bible they adorn the high priest's breastpiece, describe God's dazzling throne, and form the foundations of the new Jerusalem, a picture of God's people as precious and of a city of unimaginable glory.
44363: Twelve stones engraved with the tribes' names sat over the high priest's heart.
44364: The dazzling glory of God's throne
44365: Sapphire pavement, a throne like sapphire, jasper and carnelian, an emerald rainbow.
44366: The beauty of the new Jerusalem
44367: Foundations adorned with twelve kinds of jewels. The list echoes the high priest's breastpiece, suggesting the whole city is priestly and holy.
44369: Onyx in Eden's land; the king of Tyre in Eden covered with stones.
44371: Gold, silver and precious stones survive the testing fire; wood, hay and straw do not.
44372: The breastpiece, Solomon's temple and the wealth of kings.
44373: Mostly Revelation: the throne, Babylon's jewellery (Rev 17:4) and the city's foundations.
44374: The ancient names of gems cannot always be matched to modern stones, so translations vary. Ancient writers such as Josephus and Philo linked the twelve stones with months or signs of the zodiac; assigning each stone a fixed spiritual meaning or tribe in Revelation is speculative.
44377: Pearls were among the most costly luxuries in the Roman world. Jesus uses a pearl for the surpassing worth of God's kingdom, and Revelation makes each gate of the new Jerusalem a single pearl.
44378: The surpassing worth of the kingdom
44379: A merchant sells everything to buy one pearl. Most read the merchant as a disciple giving all for the kingdom; others read the merchant as Christ giving all to gain his people. Debated.
44380: Holy things not to be thrown away
44381: Do not throw pearls before pigs: use discernment about sharing sacred things with those who will trample them.
44383: Contrasted with good deeds; part of Babylon's wealth.
44385: Each gate is one huge pearl: lavish welcome into the city.
44386: No certain mention. Wisdom is 'more precious than peninim' (Job 28:18; Prov 3:15; Prov 8:11), a word variously translated rubies, corals or pearls.
44387: Jesus' parables and sayings, Paul's advice on modesty, and Revelation.
44388: The popular idea that the pearl gates symbolise suffering (because a pearl forms around an irritation in an oyster) is a modern devotional reflection, not something the text says.
44390: Clean white clothing was costly to keep and was worn for celebrations. In the Bible white garments picture purity and forgiveness, victory and joy, and the glory of heaven.
44392: Sins like scarlet become white as snow; robes washed white in the Lamb's blood.
44393: Victory and vindication of the faithful
44394: Martyrs and those who overcome are clothed in white.
44396: The Ancient of Days, the transfigured Jesus and angels wear dazzling white.
44398: The bride's fine linen is 'the righteous deeds of the saints'. Some stress these deeds as the fruit of grace; others link the linen to Christ's righteousness given to believers. Debated.
44401: White is the colour of snow and wool for cleansing, and of the Ancient of Days in Daniel. Priests wore white linen (Lev 16:4).
44402: Transfiguration, resurrection angels and Revelation's redeemed crowd.
44403: In the early church the newly baptised were often dressed in white garments, a practice described in fourth-century baptismal instruction; it is a tradition, not a biblical command.
44406: Sackcloth was rough cloth, usually of goat hair, used for sacks. People wore it next to the skin, often with ashes on the head, to show grief, repentance or desperate prayer.
44408: Jacob mourns Joseph; Mordecai mourns Haman's decree.
44409: Even Nineveh's king and animals wear sackcloth.
44411: Ahab humbles himself; Hezekiah prays in sackcloth.
44412: The two witnesses prophesy clothed in sackcloth.
44414: God removes sackcloth and clothes with gladness.
44415: Common in narratives of grief and in prophetic calls to repentance.
44416: Jesus says Tyre and Sidon would have repented in sackcloth and ashes; the sun becomes black as sackcloth (Rev 6:12).
44419: In Jesus' parable of the wedding feast, a guest is thrown out because he is not wearing wedding clothes. The garment stands for what fits a person to share in God's kingdom celebration, though what exactly it represents is debated.
44420: What fits a guest for the kingdom
44421: The invitation is open to all, but accepting it involves being properly clothed.
44423: Many Reformed and evangelical interpreters read the garment as Christ's righteousness received by faith ('garments of salvation', 'put on Christ').
44424: A changed life of love and good works
44425: Many Church Fathers (Augustine among them) and Catholic interpreters read it as charity or a life fitting the gospel. Many interpreters combine the two readings.
44427: The church is clothed for the wedding of the Lamb.
44428: Clothing for celebration and covenant (Isa 61:10); Zephaniah warns those dressed in 'foreign attire' on the day of the LORD's sacrifice (Zeph 1:7-8).
44429: Only in Matthew's parable, but connected to Paul's language of putting on Christ and Revelation's bride.
44430: Preachers often say the host provided wedding garments to all guests, so refusing one was an insult. Evidence for such a custom is thin (2 Kgs 10:22 is sometimes cited), so do not lean on it.
44431: Paul tells believers to put on 'the whole armour of God' to stand against evil. Each piece names a spiritual reality, such as truth, righteousness, faith and God's word. The image draws first on Isaiah, where God himself puts on armour, and probably also on the Roman soldier.
44432: God's own armour shared with his people
44433: In Isaiah God wears righteousness as a breastplate and salvation as a helmet; Paul gives this armour to believers.
44434: The struggle is spiritual, not against people
44435: The enemy is spiritual forces of evil, not flesh and blood.
44437: Truth, righteousness, readiness from the gospel of peace, faith, salvation, and the word of God.
44438: Prayer as the way to stand
44439: The passage ends with constant prayer in the Spirit.
44441: Paul uses armour imagery in other letters too.
44442: God as divine warrior (Exod 15:3; Isa 59:15-18). The Wisdom of Solomon, a book outside the Protestant canon, also describes God arming himself.
44443: Ephesians 6:10-18 is the main text; parallels in Romans, 2 Corinthians and 1 Thessalonians.
44444: Whether 'righteousness' here is God's gift of right standing or the believer's upright life is debated. Elaborate modern 'spiritual warfare' methods (naming territorial spirits and so on) go beyond what this passage describes.
44448: Israel's high priest wore special garments 'for glory and for beauty': a linen tunic, a blue robe with bells and pomegranates, an embroidered apron called the ephod, a breastpiece of twelve stones, and a turban with a gold plate reading 'Holy to the LORD'. They showed that he represented the people before God.
44450: The gold plate bore 'Holy to the LORD', so the priest carried the people's guilt in offerings.
44452: The tribes' names were on his shoulders and over his heart.
44454: The Urim and Thummim in the breastpiece were used to ask God's will. How they worked is unknown.
44456: Gideon's golden ephod became a snare; Micah made one for his private shrine.
44457: Christ the high priest and a priestly people
44458: The risen Christ wears a long robe and golden sash; believers are a royal priesthood.
44459: Exodus 28 and 39 describe the garments. Simpler linen ephods were worn by Samuel and by David when he danced before the ark (1 Sam 2:18; 2 Sam 6:14). Zechariah sees the high priest's filthy clothes replaced (Zech 3:3-5).
44460: Hebrews presents Jesus as the great high priest. John notes Jesus' seamless tunic (John 19:23), which some link to the high priest's woven robe (Exod 28:32); others see no such intention.
44461: Christian vestments developed over centuries; their link to the Levitical garments is a matter of tradition and differs between churches.
44462: To anoint is to pour or rub oil on someone. It set apart kings, priests and sometimes prophets for God's service. 'Messiah' (Hebrew) and 'Christ' (Greek) both mean 'anointed one'. Anointing was also everyday care: for guests, the sick and the dead.
44464: Saul, David and Solomon are anointed; the king is 'the LORD's anointed'.
44466: Aaron is anointed; Elijah is told to anoint Elisha.
44468: Jesus is anointed with the Spirit at his baptism and announces it in Nazareth.
44470: All believers share an anointing that teaches them.
44472: A woman anoints Jesus beforehand for burial.
44473: David refuses to harm Saul because he is 'the LORD's anointed' (1 Sam 24:6). Cyrus, a Persian, is called God's anointed (Isa 45:1).
44474: The whole title 'Christ' rests on this practice. Anointing the sick continues in James 5.
44475: 'Touch not mine anointed' (Ps 105:15; 1 Chr 16:22) is about the patriarchs, and is sometimes misused to shield leaders from accountability. Anointing in later sacraments (chrismation, confirmation, anointing of the sick) is valued in Catholic and Orthodox tradition and understood differently by Protestants.
44476: Placing hands on someone or something was a way of connecting with them: identifying with a sacrifice, passing on a blessing, commissioning a leader, praying for healing, or praying for the Spirit to come.
44478: The worshipper leaned a hand on the animal; Aaron confessed sins over the scapegoat.
44479: Jacob blesses Joseph's sons; Jesus blesses children.
44481: Joshua, the Seven, Barnabas and Saul, and Timothy were set apart this way. Warning: do not be hasty (1 Tim 5:22).
44482: Jesus and the apostles often healed by touch.
44484: In some Acts episodes the Spirit comes after hands are laid on; in others not (Acts 10:44). Whether this is a pattern for today is debated.
44486: Healing, blessing, ordination and Spirit-reception; Hebrews lists it among the church's foundational teachings (Heb 6:2).
44487: Mark 16:18 (laying hands on the sick) is in the longer ending of Mark, which many textual scholars think was added later. Whether ordination passes down an unbroken 'apostolic succession' is a Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican conviction that most other Protestants do not share.
44489: Washing removes dirt, so it naturally pictures removing sin and impurity. In the Bible washing ranges from ritual cleansing for worship, to washing hands to declare innocence, to baptism and Jesus washing his disciples' feet.
44491: Priests washed before serving; impurity was removed by washing and waiting.
44495: Pilate washes his hands of Jesus' blood.
44497: How the 'washing of regeneration' relates to water baptism is debated (see /debates/baptism).
44499: Jesus washes his disciples' feet and tells them to do likewise.
44500: Priestly washings, purity laws, and Naaman's sevenfold washing in the Jordan (2 Kgs 5:10-14).
44501: Jesus disputes Pharisaic hand-washing traditions (Mark 7:1-8), washes feet, and the saints wash their robes in the Lamb's blood (Rev 7:14).
44502: Some churches (for example many Anabaptist, Brethren and Adventist groups) practise foot-washing as an ordinance; Catholic and other churches do it on Maundy Thursday; most churches treat John 13 as an example of humble service rather than a rite.
44505: To sit at a king's right hand is to share his rule and honour. Psalm 110:1, 'The LORD says to my Lord: sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool', is the Old Testament verse most often quoted or echoed in the New Testament, applied to Jesus after his resurrection.
44507: Jesus is exalted to share God's rule over all powers.
44509: Old covenant priests stood daily; Christ sat down, because his sacrifice was complete.
44511: Christ at God's right hand intercedes for his people.
44513: Believers are seated with Christ in the heavenly places.
44515: Solomon seats his mother at his right; James and John ask for the seats beside Jesus.
44516: Psalm 110 and royal court practice (1 Kgs 2:19).
